title: SLO-1999-1-002
text:
Determining the support of a specific number of voters for candidate lists for election to the National Assembly does not signify an infringement of passive voting rights if the number of signatures required is such that it does not prevent the candidature of lists which would have at least a minimal real possibility of obtaining at least one seat in Parliament. The demand for a specific number of signatures of support only excludes from the candidature procedure non-serious candidates and candidates who have no chance of success.

The Elections to the National Assembly Act (hereinafter: "the Act") determines in the disputed Article 43:

"A political party shall determine candidates under procedures defined in its rules. The list of candidates shall be determined by secret ballot.

A political party may submit a list of candidates in each electoral unit if its list of candidates is supported by the signatures of at least three members of the National Assembly. The signatures of delegates shall be submitted on the prescribed form to the Republican Electoral Commission.

A political party may submit a list of candidates in individual electoral units if the list of candidates has been determined by members of the political party which have voting rights and permanent residence in the electoral unit, and if the list of candidates is supported by the signatures of at least 50 electors who have permanent residence in the electoral unit.

A political party may also submit a list of candidates in individual electoral units where the list of candidates has not been determined in the manner prescribed in the previous paragraph, on condition that the list of candidates is supported by the signatures of at least 100 voters who have permanent residence in the electoral unit.

Two or more political parties may propose a joint candidate list."

The valid statutory rules governing standing in elections to the National Assembly does not prevent candidates who have at least a minimal possibility of election from participating in the election. Even if a political party does not gain the support for its list of at least three members of the National Assembly, it can determine candidate lists with the support of 50 or 100 voters in an electoral unit (50 when the list is determined by members of the party in the electoral unit, and 100 when the list or lists are determined by organs of the party on a national level).

In relation to data on the average number of registered voters in an electoral unit, signatures of support must be collected from an average of 0.052%, or 0.026% of voters enrolled in an electoral unit. (According to the data of the Ministry of Internal Affairs, on 30 June 1996 there were 2.039.578 citizens in total, of whom 1.593.035 were adult. The average number of adult citizens in an electoral unit is 199.129). Such a required number of signatures of support does not prevent the participation of lists for which there exists at least a minimal possibility of obtaining a seat in the division of seats on the level of electoral units (in relation to the electoral quotient, which amounts to one eleventh of votes cast in an electoral unit) or in the division of seats on a State level (in relation to the electoral threshold of three seats. This means that the required support only excludes lists which do not have even a minimal possibility of obtaining a seat from the elections. This ensures the election can be adequately supervised and makes competition between lists which have at least a minimal chance of obtaining at least one seat in the elections easier, and prevents an unnecessary splitting of votes.

The distinction between the weight of the support of members of Parliament and voters is based on legitimate and material reasons, so it is not possible to speak of an impermissible discrimination among legal subjects. It is not a distinction based on personal circumstances (nationality, race, sex, language, belief, political or other conviction etc.) but a distinction based on the different positions of these subjects in the political system. Political parties are associations of citizens formed in order to achieve political ends (especially by proposing candidates at elections), so the legislator had material grounds for according them a special place in the election process. Members of the National Assembly are elected in direct and universal elections so it is possible - irrespective of the voting system under which they are elected - to consider that they enjoy the support of a significant part of the electoral body. Distinguishing between the weight of support of signatures of members (the signatures of three members balance the signatures of at least 800 electors) is materially grounded.

The principle of equal protection of rights in procedures before the courts, other State organs, organs of local communities and holders of public authority (Article 22 of the Constitution) does not refer to the material law governing electoral rights, and the disputed Article 43 of the Act contains material legal provisions on the conditions for standing for election. In view of this, the initiators' reference to Article 22 of the Constitution is groundless.

The provisions of the Act determine what kind of support must be obtained by a list of candidates determined by a political party in order to run for election to the National Assembly in individual electoral units are not in conflict with the principle of a democratic state, the principle of equality before the law, the principle of the equal protection of rights in proceedings, the principle of universal and equal voting rights, the right to participation in public affairs or provisions on elections of delegates to the National Assembly (Articles 1, 3.2, 14, 22, 43, 44 and 80 of the Constitution).
